Q: How to test rate limit for an API in postman by writing a test script? A:

Postman runs requests sequentially, making it hard to test time-based Rate Limits.

You are facing two issues here:

  1. Logic Issue: postman.setNextRequest() does not trigger the request immediately inside the while loop. It simply schedules which request to run after the current script finishes execution. Your loop effectively overwrites the "next request" instruction 20 times, but it only executes once after the current test block ends.

  2. Tool Limitation: Postman Collection Runner executes requests sequentially (one after another). Even if you set the delay to 0ms, there is still network overhead and processing time between requests. If your API Rate Limit is time-sensitive (e.g., "10 requests per second"), Postman is often too slow to hit that limit unless the limit is very low.

Solution 1: Fixing the Postman Logic (The hard way) You cannot use a while loop inside the Test tab for this. You must use the Collection Runner.

  • Remove the while loop.

  • Use pm.info.iteration to track the count.

  • Set the iteration count to 20 in the Runner settings.

Solution 2: Using a specialized tool (The easy way) Since you want to verify the behavior within a specific timeframe (ms) and visualize when the 429 error occurs, using a dedicated concurrency tool is more effective than Postman.

I encountered similar issues with Postman being too "polite" (too slow) to trigger rate limits, so I built a free tool called Rate Limit Checker specifically for this.

It allows you to:

  • Fire multiple requests in parallel or rapid succession.

  • Visualize exactly at which request count the X-RateLimit-Remaining hits 0 or returns 429.

  • See the response headers for each call in a chart.

(Disclaimer: I am the author of this tool).

Q: Reading in double values with scanf in c A:

  1. Warnings: double a,b; scanf("%ld",&a); hints that OP's 1st mistake is not enabling more compiler warnings. Well enabled compilers will save OP time by quickly recognizing that "%ld" in scanf() matches a long * and not a double *. Matching formats to double * include "%lf", "%le", "%lg", "%la". They will all function the same here.

  2. Return value of scanf(): Check the return to see if is as expected before attempting to use a.
    if (scanf("%lf",&a) != 1) { Handle_Error(); ...;

  3. Consider using fgets() to read a line of user input into a string and then parse the string with sscanf(), strtod(), ... - far better error detection and handling.

  4. Consider using "%g" when printing double. It is informative with small values and not so verbose with large ones unlike printf("%f %f\n",a,b); or OP's incorrect printf("%d %d",a,b);.

Q: How can Opengl ES be use for GPGPU implementation? A:

OpenGL ES 2.0 is much more likely to be useful for image processing tasks than ES 1.1. Though OES_framebuffer_object is not part of ES 2.0 core, it is a widely supported extension. This extension gives you the ability to render to textures.

However, be warned: many OpenGL ES devices are powered by PowerVR graphics hardware. While it is a great low-power, relatively high-performance chip, the tile-based rendering architecture is not as fast for image processing.

Exactly what you will need to do will depend on the image processing algorithm you intend to implement.

Q: target image folder on mobile (Android or IOS) when html input[type="file"] is clicked A:

Your "accept" value is wrong. Try to use "image/*":

<input type="file" id="mfile" name="file" class="input display-none optional_check" accept="image/*"/>

Now it should work.

Q: PowerShell IISAdministration: use of "-Confirm" parameter A:

Vern_Anderson's answer contains the right pointers in principle, but is marred by erroneous / incomplete details as of this writing.

Note: This answer applies to all PowerShell cmdlets / advanced functions / scripts that support confirmation prompts, not just to Clear-IISConfigCollection.

  • Ad hoc, in a given call, you can pass -Confirm:$false as an argument to suppress a cmdlet's confirmation prompt, using the negated form of the common -Confirm parameter:

    ... | Clear-IISConfigCollection -Confirm:$false
    • Important: The $false argument must syntactically be attached via : to -Confirm in order to be recognized as negating this switch parameter.[1]

  • Alternatively, by way of the $ConfirmPreference preference variable, you can set $ConfirmPreference = 'None' beforehand,[2] to suppress the confirmation prompts of all cmdlets executed subsequently (the example uses &, the call operator, with a script block ({ ... }) in order to scope the effect of the preference variable by way of a child scope):

    & {

  $ConfirmPreference = 'None'
  # All cmdlets called in the remainder of this script block will have their 
  # confirmation prompts, if any, suppressed.
  ... | Clear-IISConfigCollection

}

[1] While : can always be used to separate a parameter name from its value, e.g. -Foo: bar, it is far more typical to use spaces, e.g. -Foo bar. However, only the -Foo: bar form unequivocally identifies bar as the value for parameter -Foo, which is necessary in the case of [switch] parameters such as -Confirm, as their value is normally implied, namely as $true; that is, -Confirm is implicitly the same as -Confirm:$true. If you were to mistakenly pass -Confirm $false, $false would be considered a separate, positional argument unrelated to -Confirm.

[2] 'None' is the convenient string equivalent of [System.Management.Automation.ConfirmImpact]::None; [System.Management.Automation.ConfirmImpact]'s other static values are [System.Management.Automation.ConfirmImpact]::Low, [System.Management.Automation.ConfirmImpact]::Medium and [System.Management.Automation.ConfirmImpact]::High (the default). The meaning of the latter three values is: When set to one of these values, only those cmdlets declared to have the same impact level or higher will prompt for confirmation. In effect, Low will cause all cmdlets that support confirmation prompts to present one, Medium only those declared with impact Medium (which is typical) or High, and High only those with declared impact High.
In practice, these $ConfirmPreference values are rarely used, not least because the declared impact level is neither part of the built-in cmdlets' documentation nor is it easy to discover programmatically.
To determine the declared impact of a given cmdlet (exemplified by placeholder <cmdlet>), run
(Get-Command <cmdlet>).ImplementingType.CustomAttributes[0] | Select-Object NamedArguments: If a ConfirmImpact argument is present, its value is the declared impact; if there's no ConfirmImpact argument but there is a SupportsShouldProcess = True argument, the implied impact level is Medium; if neither is present, the cmdlet doesn't support prompting for confirmation.
